ai-9d81fbefc4.headline: Musk Claims SpaceX Closed $40 Billion Debt Deal for AI Chips
ai-9d81fbefc4.fulltext:
[Text below is Semafor's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Elon Musk said SpaceX has closed a $40 billion debt deal to pay for the chips it needs to fuel its artificial intelligence ambitions.
SpaceX finalized the debt raise to pay for Nvidia Corp.’s graphics processing units, or GPUs, thanks to its investment-grade ratings and revenue from its Starlink satellite business and rocket launches, Musk wrote in a post on X, discussing the off-balance-sheet deal.
SpaceX’s $40 billion debt raise is being finalized at sharply higher interest rates than when the rocket company last tapped bondholders, a sign of growing jitters in the AI world.
The lowest-rated portion is expected to carry interest rates of about 8.3%, according to people familiar with the deal, which is being led by Apollo and Goldman Sachs. A safer piece of debt, which is backed by some of SpaceX’s chips, is likely to price next week around 7.75%, the people said. That is more than 1 percentage point more than where SpaceX’s current bonds trade, reflecting an AI-loan market that has pulled back sharply over the past few weeks. President Donald Trump purchased $5 million in SpaceX bonds in August.
Goldman and Apollo declined to comment. Pricing could change by the time the debt is finalized, which is expected sometime next week.
Existing bonds at SpaceX, which is currently considering merging with Tesla, have weakened in recent days as strong earnings were overshadowed by massive spending plans and concerns about the company’s debt load, plus broader AI fears fueled by CoreWeave’s debt selloff. Default insurance on the company also widened, signaling some misgivings on the company’s plans.

ai-7241bd68f0.headline: Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark moves his prediction for self-improving AI forward to 2027
ai-7241bd68f0.fulltext:
Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark moves his prediction for self-improving AI forward to 2027
A new benchmark called TasteVal measures how well AI systems design experiments on their own and interpret the results. The findings show an unusually steep improvement curve.
That capability has roughly doubled every three months since December 2025, according to Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark. The research lab P-Zero Research calls it "research taste," meaning the ability to pick the right experiments and draw the right conclusions from them. The best model tested outperformed a comparison group of 24 human experts at a fraction of the cost.
Clark co-founded Anthropic and writes the Import AI newsletter. Based on the numbers, he now believes recursive self-improvement (RSI), where AI systems develop their own successors, could become possible as early as 2027. He had previously expected 2028.
The benchmark doesn't prove that AI systems are already improving themselves, since it only captures a narrow slice of scientific work. But it does show where the debate is heading, away from raw model performance and toward the question of how much independent research work language models can actually take on.
TasteVal only measures part of the picture
P-Zero Research defines research taste as three abilities: identifying which research questions are worth pursuing, designing experiments to answer them, and correctly interpreting the results. TasteVal only tests the last two. Choosing the most promising research direction is often considered the core of scientific intuition, but in TasteVal that decision is already made for the model.
Each of the eight tasks specifies a fixed research goal from AI model development, along with a measurable score. The tasks cover areas like training data selection, pretraining and fine-tuning language models, training on human preferences, and defending against adversarial prompts.
The model decides which experiment to run next and uses the results to guide its following step. To keep coding skill from skewing the outcome, a fixed coding agent runs all experiments on a single Nvidia H100 GPU. Each run ends after 40 GPU-hours of compute or 120 hours of wall-clock time.
The human baseline came from 24 experts who had recently worked at places like OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Nvidia, and Microsoft Research. They tackled the same tasks, with at least two people on each one. The best human attempt per task served as the benchmark.
Research taste measured through compute efficiency
To make research taste quantifiable, P-Zero Research translates it into compute efficiency. The reasoning is that experiment compute is scarce in AI research, so picking the right experiments and reading their results correctly means fewer runs and more progress on the same budget.
The lab draws on its "AI Futures Model," which predicts that experiment compute becomes the biggest bottleneck once coding is automated. So TasteVal measures how much compute a model needs to match the experts' scores. A model that gets there with half the compute has twice the research taste by this definition. P-Zero Research calls this ratio the compute multiplier.
The top model, Anthropic's Opus 5.5, hit a compute multiplier of 2.3, reaching expert-level scores with less than half the compute. The statistical range runs from 1.15 to 4.37, though. At the low end, the model would barely lead. A single run cost roughly one-thirtieth of what an expert attempt cost on average.
Across several model generations, the compute multiplier has roughly doubled every three months since December 2025. The uncertainty is large here too, with the reported doubling time ranging from 1.7 to 5.0 months.
In prior years, model research taste grew much more slowly. The curve only steepened around the turn of 2025 into 2026. Whether that's a lasting trend can't be determined from a single benchmark, and the authors themselves admit their results may overstate "how quickly research taste is improving." The tasks can be checked quickly and cheaply, which is the kind of task AI labs find easiest to optimize for. The comparison group also didn't include any top-tier researchers.
Clark pulls his timeline forward
Clark has long called creativity the key factor in how fast AI systems can improve themselves. Earlier this year, he wrote that models hadn't shown this ability at any groundbreaking scale. He now points to progress in mathematical breakthroughs and benchmarks like TasteVal as signs that this is changing.
In a long essay in May, Clark had offered more cautious numbers. He put the odds of a system that independently trains a stronger successor at roughly 60 percent by the end of 2028 and 30 percent by 2027. That forecast comes from someone who co-founded the company whose model tops the benchmark, which adds a layer of bias to the prediction.
Critics had drawn the line at exactly this capability
TasteVal matters because it measures the exact capability that skeptics had flagged as a barrier to a major AI breakthrough. AI researcher Herbie Bradley pushed back on Clark's May essay, arguing that while models could plausibly take over the work of junior researchers, more demanding skills like research taste, creativity, and coherent long-term research planning were nowhere in sight.
When it comes to planning and evaluating experiments, TasteVal pushes against that assessment, though it says nothing about choosing a long-term research agenda.
How wide the practical gap remains shows up in a study on AI development using AI agents led by a team at Fudan University. The researchers analyzed the development of their own model and found that AI agents contributed up to 55 percent of methodology proposals, but humans still made over 85 percent of the final decisions. The authors noted it remains unclear how AI can generate diverse research directions and assess their value before results are in, and that's exactly the kind of decision TasteVal takes off the models' plate.
The debate is shifting
The benchmark arrives in the middle of a debate the major AI labs kicked off themselves. In June, Anthropic wrote that recursive self-improvement hasn't been achieved yet but "could come sooner than most institutions are prepared for" Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei now calls for a controlled slowdown in AI development, while OpenAI acknowledges that fully autonomous RSI isn't happening yet and says it should only be pursued if human oversight is guaranteed.
TasteVal shifts what counts as progress. For a long time, the focus was on how well models solve well-defined tasks like math problems or coding challenges, but now the question is increasingly whether they can make the decisions that push research forward.
If the trend P-Zero Research measured holds up in other tests, the implications cut both ways. AI development would get faster and cheaper, but at the same time a growing share of the research would become harder for humans to verify, because models would be planning and evaluating their own experiments.

Artificial intelligence's next big bottleneck in India is a very small chip
Funding is flowing, but the country's AI builders are struggling to secure the chips, memory, and power needed to train and run models

7 min read  Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 10:11 PM IST
Listen to This Article
Capital is no longer the only thing standing between India’s artificial intelligence (AI) companies and the computing power their projects need. Venture-backed startups often receive free Cloud credits on top of their funding, while established firms can pay for compute from their own cash flows. What neither can get quickly enough are the chips.
An entire engineering team can lose a quarter waiting for graphics processing units (GPUs), the specialised chips used to train and run AI models. Deliveries can take three to four months, investors and founders say.
“Early-stage startups get credit so compute affordability is not an issue in the first year. However, the challenge with AI compute is not just affordability, but access,” said Rahul Agarwalla, managing partner at SenseAI Ventures.
“With demand outstripping supply, companies are increasingly looking to secure capacity in advance. Three-year commitments are better to get capacity, but it’s difficult for startups to accurately forecast demand,” he added.
Established startups such as payments technology platform Juspay can afford to front-load investments in securing compute, but they face the same queue when procuring GPUs.
The Bengaluru-based financial technology company swung to a net loss of ₹90 crore in 2025-26, after posting its first annual net profit of ₹62 crore, as it stepped up spending on AI infrastructure and overseas expansion.
“I wish I could spend more on GPUs, and I say that because it is hard to get GPUs allocated. Right now, I don’t have enough GPUs, and I am bottlenecked. I have been given commitments that it will take three to six months to come,” Juspay Cofounder and Chief Operating Officer Sheetal Lalwani said during a media briefing this month.
Across India’s AI ecosystem, founders and venture capital investors describe the same paradox: the constraint has shifted from what a company can afford to what it can actually get.
A chip delay, a quarter lost
Ashish Taneja, founding partner and chief executive officer (CEO) of growX ventures, said, “When a GPU card takes three or four months to arrive, a whole engineering team can lose a quarter, and that hurts far more than a chip being a generation old.”
Compute affordability is generally not an issue for startups in their first year, given the Cloud credits they receive, Agarwalla said.
Gokul N A, founder of growX-backed robotics company CynLr, said, “After you order a GPU card, you may wait three or four months, and the whole team waits with it. Pricing on industrial-grade chipsets fluctuates too, sometimes by 2x or 3x.”
Rent by the token, or own the machine?
The answer lies in how AI is billed.
Frontier AI laboratories (labs) such as OpenAI and Anthropic charge by the token, a small unit of text that an AI model reads or generates. The bill therefore rises with usage.
Heavy workloads such as AI-assisted coding, in which models read and rewrite large volumes of code, can consume tokens quickly.
Subscription plans offer a fixed allowance, but Lalwani said those allowances are “already one-fifth of their peak today” as providers try to make the plans pay. “Those subs have to make sense eventually,” he said.
The alternative is to run freely available open-source models on GPUs a company controls. The cost then stays fixed regardless of how much the models are used. Juspay runs about 95 per cent of its AI-assisted coding this way.
“Renting an 8-node GPU costs ₹25-35 lakh a month, while buying the same work as tokens from frontier labs could be even 5x, 10x that cost,” he said.
Agarwalla agreed that “dedicated or leased infrastructure can become more cost-effective as workloads grow and utilisation becomes predictable”.
Taneja cautioned, however, that most startups building applications should still rent. Buying GPUs too early, he said, “locks capital into hardware that’ll be out of date before the product has found its market”.
The bottleneck behind the bottleneck
“Chip and component supply have been a challenge from the pandemic days through this AI boom,” said Srinivas Shekar, founder and CEO of data-security firm Pantherun.
The company now designs around several suppliers so that no single vendor can hold up a delivery.
Lalwani said the bottlenecks extend beyond GPUs themselves. The first is memory. Advanced AI chips rely on high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which is stacked close to the processor to feed it data fast enough to keep it working.
Only three companies — SK hynix, Samsung, and Micron — produce HBM at scale. Micron said in December 2025 that its entire 2026 HBM supply had been committed, while SK hynix said in October 2025 that it had secured demand for all its memory chips for 2026.
The second constraint is power and data-centre space.
A GPU is useful only when installed in a facility that can supply continuous power and keep it cool, unlike an ordinary server. Outside India, procuring GPUs is harder because data centre capacity and power have largely been committed to hyperscalers, Lalwani said.
He warned that even in India, larger players could lock up data centre capacity and power in the future, even if chip procurement eases over the next 12 months.
A public pool, private constraints
The government’s IndiaAI Mission has onboarded more than 38,000 GPUs that startups and researchers can rent at subsidised rates. Taneja said the pool “has scaled faster than almost anyone predicted, and for training language models in a data centre it does the job”.
Some companies, however, need compute in a different form.
“Think about how long a WhatsApp message sometimes takes to arrive, and now imagine that delay when the arm has to stop before it hits a wall. The compute has to sit right next to the robot, physically wired in. So we’re forced to train robots live and keep our compute local,” Gokul said.
Defence technology firm Armory cannot run its workloads on shared servers for security reasons. “The IndiaAI pool would work much better for us if it offered dedicated rack space as metal-as-a-service, similar to the Equinix model, where the provider manages power, cooling, and connectivity and the customer manages the control plane. Offering only AI compute also isn’t ideal. A defence technology company runs many kinds of workloads, and splitting them across providers adds overhead,” a spokesperson for the company said.
Beyond the cheque: Can they get compute?
Taneja said compute can account for half or more of a funding round at a company training its own foundation model, compared with 10 to 20 per cent at a company building applications on other models.
In robotics, the arithmetic is harsher.
Gokul estimated that running a robot the way large language models run today could cost “two to three million dollars per robot per year”, compared with $230,000 a year for a worker across three shifts. “Nobody will adopt that,” he said.
Despite the waiting times and costs, companies are looking to invest further in the space.
Lalwani said Juspay funds its GPU purchases from its own cash flows and balance sheet and wants to deploy more capital. But, as Agarwalla put it, “The question is not simply how much compute a company can afford, but whether it can access the right capacity and use it efficiently.” 
The hurdles 
- With demand outstripping supply, companies are increasingly looking to secure capacity in advance
- When a GPU card takes 3-4 months to arrive, a whole engineering team can lose a quarter
- Procurement of GPUs is harder outside India
- Dedicated or leased infrastructure can become more cost-effective as workloads grow

indian-startups-7ec739c0d3.headline: Flipkart’s Summer Of Discontent
indian-startups-7ec739c0d3.fulltext: Questions over an IPO and ESOPs, huge investments in quick commerce and food delivery and the pressure to deliver profits: Flipkart is juggling one too many hot potatoes for the past year. In that time, the ecommerce giant has seen 14 senior level exits, including three more VPs who are set to leave the company next. The latest executives to leave are Kanchan Mishra, VP of smartphones; Amit Sachan, VP of product and tech; and Kamal Chopra, VP of corporate, as Moneycontrol reported. While Mishra spent more than a decade at Flipkart, Sachan and Chopra have been with the company for four and five years, respectively. As their tenure shows these are not employees who had just joined the company one or two years ago in the wake of all the IPO talk. These were executives who had seen much of the restructuring at Flipkart in the post-pandemic years. Plus, these departures come at a time when the company’s employees have raised concerns over ESOP liquidity and the company’s long-awaited IPO remains without a firm timeline. It has coloured these exits with a darker tint as a result. Walmart has reportedly asked the company to prioritise profitability before going public, while the expansion of its quick commerce business, Flipkart Minutes, requires significant ongoing investments. Employees holding stock options, meanwhile, are waiting for an opportunity to cash out. Sources told Inc42 that some of these executives left as they were unable to see a clear opportunity to liquidate their ESOPs, while others moved to new jobs or wanted to start their own ventures. It must be noted that at this middle management level, Flipkart has around 30 executives in VP roles and more than a dozen senior vice presidents, so these departures will not necessarily destabilise the company, but it is a sign of bubbling discontent. ESOP Liquidity Dispute Widens In fact, sources told us that the frustration over stock options has moved beyond internal discussions, with former senior executives approaching Walmart’s board to seek a fair opportunity to realise the value of their vested ESOPs. Earlier this month, former Flipkart executives, including ex-Myntra CEO Mukesh Bansal, former chief business officer Ankit Nagori and former CFO Sanjay Baweja, wrote to Walmart’s board seeking fair treatment and a full cash-out opportunity for their vested options simply because they left the company. The issue has gained importance because an IPO has long been seen as a potential exit route for employees holding Flipkart shares or options. With the listing pushed back, those employees have little clarity on when they can realise that value. For senior executives who have spent a year at Flipkart, the delay also affects decisions about whether to stay or pursue opportunities elsewhere. While ESOP liquidity is one reason behind some departures, the company’s leadership churn is also a result of executives moving into new roles or setting up their own ventures. The founder of a unicorn startup with over 30,000 employees told us that while Flipkart has the responsibility of providing liquidity to employees, listing in a hurry to meet these demands would be a mistake. “At the end of the day, Flipkart’s management and Walmart have to do the right thing by the company. If they have already done a $50 Mn ESOP buy back last year, then they already provided some liquidity opportunity. If an employee has already made ₹10 Cr - ₹15 Cr through that, then they need to give the company some more time for the next event. But if an employee who has made a few lakhs of rupees via the buyback is upset, then the management needs to address that. What’s the point of listing in a rush, without getting a good market value?” the founder said on the condition of anonymity. Walmart Wants Profit Before IPO The fact is that Flipkart’s listing plans have been discussed for years, but the immediate priority appears to be improving its financial performance. In May 2026, Moneycontrol reported that parent Walmart wanted Flipkart to achieve EBITDA breakeven by the end of FY27 before considering an IPO or another external fundraise. The report said the decision followed Walmart CEO John Furner’s visit to Bengaluru. The reported directive adds another hurdle for a company that completed its reverse flip from Singapore to India in March 2026, ahead of a potential domestic listing. There is the looming valuation question. Flipkart currently commands a valuation of $35 Bn - $36 Bn and earlier was eyeing a valuation of $50 Bn. This valuation expectation complicates finding the right window for the listing. Walmart can afford to wait for improved financial performance which would justify the valuation, but that’s not the case with employees seeking liquidity. “In a current situation, getting a $50 Bn valuation will be extremely difficult. It is indeed a tricky position for the company,” the founder quoted above added. Others believe that Flipkart cannot go into an IPO with the narrative of a growth-at-all-costs tech startup. The company is far too mature for this. “Flipkart will likely face pushback and could be forced into a valuation haircut to land in the $25B–$30 Bn range. This will match global tech-retail multiples,” Rahul Sharma, Head of Research at Equity99 said. On the other hand, the company can position itself as a disciplined, maturing omnichannel ecosystem. “A concrete roadmap to profitability can successfully defend the $35 Bn mark that Flipkart is said to be seeking,” he added. The delay is particularly striking because other Indian ecommerce companies have already reached the public markets. Meesho listed on the NSE and BSE on December 10, 2025, following a ₹5,421 Cr IPO. Snapdeal’s parent, AceVector, listed on October 5, 2026, after a ₹420 Cr public issue. Their listing gives investors a way to set benchmarks for ecommerce, while Flipkart continues to work towards its own debut. However, the comparison also shows that going public does guarantee a strong market reception. AceVector shares listed at an issue price of ₹32 and subsequently traded below that level. For Flipkart, the question is whether stronger financial performance can support its valuation expectations without forcing the company to slow its growth plans. Flipkart Minutes Complicates Profitability Push The push to improve profitability comes amid Flipkart’s aggressive investments in quick commerce. Flipkart Minutes has expanded its dark store network to compete with Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart and Zepto. The business gives Flipkart a way to serve customers looking for rapid delivery of groceries, electronics and other everyday products. However, the expansion requires spending on dark stores, inventory, fulfillment and delivery operations. New stores need time to build order volumes and improve their economics. Until a store reaches sufficient throughput, its operating costs can weigh on the business. Flipkart Minutes has scaled to 1,000 micro fulfillment centers across 130+ cities and 8,000+ pincodes in under two years. The current scale of Minutes’ spending is not publicly disclosed. However, its expansion presents a challenge for Flipkart as Walmart reportedly seeks EBITDA breakeven before an IPO. Now, Flipkart is preparing to enter another competitive market with its food delivery service branded eat-in by Minutes. Currently available for its 8,000 employees, will soon be available to the public by the end of this month. The food delivery business could add to Flipkart’s spending requirements. The company reportedly will use a dedicated delivery fleet through its logistics arm Ekart. Moreover, it will also require onboard restaurants and attract customers in a market where established players spend on discounts, promotions and customer acquisition. These costs could build before the service reaches sufficient order volumes to support its operations. The launch puts Flipkart in the position of investing in two businesses that require scale to improve their economics, even as Walmart reportedly wants the group to reach EBITDA breakeven before an IPO. While food delivery could bring more frequent customer visits to Flipkart’s app, it will also require spending to compete with established platforms. Losses Grow, Pressure Builds Flipkart’s financial performance will also remain under scrutiny as it works towards a potential IPO. The Flipkart Group reported an 18.2% YoY increase in consolidated revenue from operation to ₹1.45 Lakh Cr in FY26, compared with ₹1.23 Lakh Cr in FY25. Its consolidated net loss narrowed marginally by 2.1% to ₹8,468 Cr from ₹8,646 Cr in the previous year. The financial results cover the wider Flipkart Group, including Myntra, Cleartrip, logistics, and other business, rather than the ecommerce marketplace alone. The group said its gross margins rose 23% during FY26, while adjusted EBITDA improved by around ₹1,500 Cr. Adjusted operating margin improved by 230 basis points, from -7.7% to -5.4%, while adjusted operating business losses narrowed by 17%, or around ₹1,600 Cr. However, the improvement in operating performance translated into only a modest reduction in net loss. Higher finance cost, the recognition of deferred tax assets and certain exceptional items weighed on the bottom line. The ecommerce vertical, Flipkart Internet, reported a 19.3% YoY decline in revenue from operations to ₹16,295 Cr in FY26. Its net loss rose to ₹5,498 Cr from ₹1,694 Cr in FY25. A significant portion of that is likely due to the redomiciling to India which was completed in March 2026. As Flipkart works on its public market plans, the combination of profitability targets, valuation expectations and employee concerns over stock liquidity is likely to remain in focus. For senior executives weighing their next move, the absence of a firm IPO timeline leaves questions unanswered: when will the equity they have accumulated at Flipkart become liquid wealth? deep-tech-014a402c71.headline: ISRO to have four launch pads by 2029, says Narayanan
deep-tech-014a402c71.fulltext:
ISRO Chairman V. Narayanan has said that India will expand its space operations significantly with four functional launch pads by 2029.
He outlined the agency's roadmap, which includes a 2,000-acre dedicated Small Satellite Launch Vehicle (SSLV) complex at Kulasekarapattinam in Tuticorin district to meet the global demand for satellite deployment.
Clarifying that the national space agency will not be privatised, Mr. Narayanan emphasised that partnering with private firms was essential to meet surging global and domestic demands for thousands of satellites.
"To handle this expanding ecosystem, ISRO will handhold startups and private enterprises, transferring technological expertise to foster economic growth and generate thousands of high-tech jobs," he said while speaking at a graduation ceremony at a private university here on Saturday (October 24, 2026).
"India will expand its space operations significantly with four functional launch pads by 2029, supported by an increasing reliance on private industry partnerships to handle commercial operations," Mr. Narayanan said.
The ISRO chief said that the upcoming Kulasekarapattinam spaceport facility will feature crucial infrastructure such as integration buildings, launch pads, rail-track systems, telemetry, tracking, and command systems.
Stating that ISRO plans to conduct the first uncrewed Gaganyaan test within the next two months, followed by two subsequent uncrewed tests before the crewed mission, he said, "These tests will evaluate environmental control, safety systems, crew escape mechanisms, and module interiors under varying pressure, temperature, and humidity conditions."
He said ISRO successfully conducted approximately 8,000 ground-based experiments for the mission, and four astronaut-designates are currently undergoing specialised training.
Looking further ahead, Mr. Narayanan revealed plans for Chandrayaan-5, a collaborative lunar mission with Japan's space agency featuring a 350-kg rover designed to conduct 100 days of surface experiments.

health-tech-e3c1c7d3ee.headline: STAT+: After a cancer vaccine’s first success, the race is on to expand the impact
health-tech-e3c1c7d3ee.fulltext:
MADRID — With the first pivotal trial showing a customized mRNA treatment improved outcomes for cancer patients presented here this weekend, the conversation has already turned to how melanoma specialists should adopt the medicine — and how widely these novel vaccines can be deployed.
“In principle, this type of approach may be applicable to other types of tumors,” James Larkin of London’s Royal Marsden Hospital, the scientific co-chair for this year’s European Society for Medical Oncology meeting, said at an opening press conference.
The trial, from Merck and Moderna, demonstrated that the bespoke mRNA-based vaccine intismeran reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 42% when combined with Merck’s checkpoint inhibitor Keytruda versus Keytruda alone. The results are a clear victory for the field after what Vinod Balachandran of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center called in a lecture a “long and sordid” history of trying to develop cancer vaccines that, until now, has essentially added up to 100 years of failure.

india-bd103bb014.headline: India-EU FTA Set For Year-End Seal, Operational Rollout Slated For Q1 Next Year: Piyush Goyal
india-bd103bb014.fulltext:
Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal expects the India-EU Free Trade Agreement to be operationalised by the end of 2026, with the pact taking effect in the first quarter of 2027. His remarks came during a visit to the Netherlands.
Goyal's Netherlands visit also focused on logistics cooperation and opportunities for Indian exporters.
Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal has said the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA) is expected to be operationalised by the end of 2026, with the pact coming into effect in the first quarter of 2027.
Speaking during an interaction with the Indian diaspora in Amsterdam on October 25, Goyal outlined the expected timeline for implementing the agreement, which is anticipated to open new opportunities for businesses and strengthen commercial ties between India and Europe.
The minister's remarks came during his visit to the Netherlands, where he held engagements focused on trade, investment and logistics cooperation. He also visited the Port of Rotterdam, Europe's largest port, and met its chief executive, Boudewijn Siemons.
Rotterdam's strategic position as a gateway to European markets could become increasingly significant as Indian exporters prepare to tap opportunities arising from the trade agreement.
The port's logistics infrastructure and international connectivity offer scope to strengthen cargo movement and India-Europe supply chains.
Goyal has also highlighted discussions between Indian customs authorities and Rotterdam port officials on digitalising cargo processes in India. The proposed cooperation aims to accelerate cargo evacuation, reduce ship turnaround times and improve operational efficiency.
During his interaction with the Indian community, Goyal expressed concern over young people being influenced by what he described as negativity and the abandonment of traditional value systems in some European countries.
"Unfortunately, youth are getting swayed by some negativity," he said, adding that young people needed to become more responsive and responsible.
He also emphasised that Indians were peace-loving and contributed positively to the countries in which they lived and worked.
The diaspora gathering brought together around 70 participants, including business and professional representatives, at an event hosted by the Indian Embassy in Amsterdam.
Goyal's visit underscores India's efforts to deepen economic engagement with the Netherlands as preparations for the India-EU FTA advance. The agreement's implementation timeline and the development of efficient logistics links will be important factors for businesses seeking to expand trade between the two markets.

Avg India oil prices hit 15-year high: Threaten OMC margins, strain Centre
The oil price surge is putting pressure on fuel retailers and government finances, raising concerns over inflation and a widening fiscal deficit
 premium 
7 min read  Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 11:20 PM IST
Listen to This Article
The surge in the price of India’s crude oil basket to a nearly 15-year high threatens to squeeze oil marketing companies’ (OMCs’) margins, stoke inflationary concerns and add to the Centre’s fiscal pressures amid mounting fertiliser subsidy costs. The basket averaged around $120 a barrel in October so far, its highest level since March 2012, when it averaged $123.61 a barrel. 
For India, which relies heavily on imported crude, a prolonged price surge could widen the current account deficit (CAD), increase the cost of shielding consumers from higher fuel prices and leave the government with less fiscal room. OMCs continue to face under-recoveries despite retail fuel price increases in May, while the fertiliser subsidy bill could exceed the FY27 Budget Estimate by more than 76 per cent if the current trajectory persists. 
The extent of the economic fallout will depend on how long crude prices remain elevated, particularly over the next three months, economists said. 
“If crude oil prices remain elevated for the next three months, the immediate effect would be visible on wholesale inflation as manufacturers would bear the high input price,” said Madan Sabnavis, chief economist at Bank of Baroda. “However, I wouldn’t expect manufacturers to pass on the burden to consumers until the festive season ends.” 
Wholesale price index-based inflation, which had hovered close to 10 per cent since May, rose to 11.4 per cent in September. Sustained input-cost pressures could eventually feed into retail inflation, depending on companies’ pricing decisions and demand conditions. “Overall, India’s retail inflation may hover around 5-6 per cent in the coming quarter,” Sabnavis said.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) raised its projection for consumer price index (CPI)-based inflation to 5.2 per cent from 5 per cent this month. The Monetary Policy Committee also hiked the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5 per cent and shifted its stance to “calibrated tightening” from neutral. 
OMC losses, fuel prices add to fiscal strain 
OMCs remain caught between rising international crude prices and the difficulty of passing on the higher costs to consumers. Although petrol and diesel prices are technically deregulated, state-owned retailers have at times kept pump prices unchanged despite sharp movements in global crude prices, putting pressure on their marketing margins. 
OMCs raised retail fuel prices by around ₹7.50 a litre in four tranches in May. However, with crude prices crossing $100 a barrel after the West Asia war began, the companies have continued to face under-recoveries. 
“Even after the hike in retail prices of fuel, OMCs are recording under-recoveries,” said Madhavi Arora, chief economist at Emkay Global. “OMCs may require extra support if the under-recoveries continue in the third quarter  as well.” 
The losses have widened since September. On September 23, Icra had estimated under-recoveries of ₹8 per litre on petrol and ₹9 per litre on diesel. The under-recovery on diesel has since doubled to around ₹20 per litre, said Prashant Vasisht, vice-president and co-head of corporate ratings at Icra. 
“OMCs are looking at the sustenance in crude oil prices. The geopolitical condition is very volatile right now and everyone is waiting for a breakthrough. However, if energy prices remain elevated at these levels, the firms might have to consider raising retail fuel prices for consumers,” Vasisht said. 
Equirus Securities had earlier warned that sustained crude prices above $100 a barrel could pressure OMC finances, particularly if petrol, diesel and LPG prices remain unchanged. The impact would depend on retail-price pass-through, government policies and refining cracks. 
Among the major OMCs, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation is the most vulnerable because its refining-to-marketing ratio is only 51 per cent, compared with 74 per cent for Bharat Petroleum Corporation and 80 per cent for Indian Oil Corporation. 
The government has already cut the special additional excise duty on petrol and diesel by ₹10 a litre to ease the pressure on OMCs. But the move has come at a cost to the exchequer. The Centre’s excise duty collections contracted nearly 23 per cent year-on-year to ₹86,687 crore in April-August, according to the latest available data. The scope for another duty cut appears limited amid pressure on revenue collections. 
The possibility of further retail fuel price increases may also be constrained by the approaching Uttar Pradesh Assembly election. Any delay in passing on higher international costs would prolong the pressure on OMC margins. 
Fertiliser subsidies compound fiscal pressures 
The Centre faces a parallel fiscal challenge from fertiliser subsidies. More than 58 per cent of the FY27 Budget Estimate of ₹1.70 trillion had already been exhausted in the first five months of the financial year. If the current trajectory continues, the bill could exceed the allocation by more than 76 per cent, reaching around ₹3 trillion. This would be the highest annual fertiliser subsidy bill on record. 
There has been some relief on the input-cost front, with urea prices falling from nearly $950 a tonne to around $390 a tonne between May and September 2026. However, persistently high di-ammonium phosphate (DAP) and sulphur prices could limit the decline in the overall subsidy burden. 
Natural gas, a key raw material for urea production, has become substantially more expensive, rising from around $10 per million British thermal units (MMBtu) before the West Asia war to more than $28-29 per MMBtu afterwards. This could offset some of the relief from lower urea prices, limiting the scope for a significant reduction in the fertiliser subsidy bill. 
India consumes around 70 million tonnes of fertilisers annually, with urea accounting for approximately 40 million tonnes.
The combined pressure from oil-related support and fertiliser subsidies could complicate the government’s fiscal calculations. Sabnavis expects the fiscal deficit to reach 4.6 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP), against the Budget projection of 4.3 per cent. 
“As OMCs register losses, the dividend revenue from them is likely to be nil for the government. Some support may come from disinvestment receipts, but fertiliser and oil subsidy may complicate the fiscal math,” he said. 
Prolonged oil shock could weigh on growth 
The risks extend beyond inflation and government finances to economic growth. In March, shortly after the West Asia war began, Chief Economic Adviser (CEA) V Anantha Nageswaran told Parliament’s Standing Committee on Finance that GDP growth could slow to 6.4 per cent in FY27 if crude oil prices rose to $130 a barrel and stayed there for two to three quarters.
Under that scenario, retail inflation could rise to 5.5 per cent, the CAD could widen to 3.2 per cent of GDP and the Centre’s fiscal deficit could increase to 5.6 per cent of GDP, Nageswaran had said. 
By contrast, the CEA’s scenario analysis suggested that the macroeconomic impact would be limited if crude prices remained around $90 a barrel. At that level, GDP growth was projected at 7-7.4 per cent, with retail inflation at around 2 per cent. The CAD was estimated at 1-1.2 per cent of GDP and the fiscal deficit at 4.3-4.4 per cent of GDP. 
The Indian crude basket averaged $101.31 a barrel in the first quarter of FY27 (April-June) and $96.11 a barrel in the second quarter. 
The higher prices have also pushed up India's import bill. Crude oil imports rose 46.4 per cent to $90.6 billion in April-September 2026-27, while the net oil and gas bill increased 35 per cent to $81.1 billion. 
In FY23, when the Russia-Ukraine war disrupted global energy markets, India's average CPI inflation rose to 6.7 per cent, above the RBI's upper tolerance limit of 6 per cent. 
A prolonged period of elevated crude prices could once again test India's ability to absorb an external shock while containing inflation, limiting the strain on public finances and protecting growth.

Serbia has entered a new political era after Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to a historic student-led protest movement in an election on Sunday, bringing an end to his long grip on power.
The streets of Belgrade erupted in celebration following Vucic's announcement, as drivers sounded their car horns and students chanted "victory" and "he's done".
The snap elections came following nearly two years of student-driven demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism, which were triggered when a train station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in 2024, killing 16 people.

ai-d399085249.headline: Anthropic sued for allegedly using 274 Elvis Presley songs to train AI models
ai-d399085249.fulltext:
The owners of Elvis Presley’s music catalogue are suing artificial intelligence (AI) company Anthropic for allegedly using Presley’s songs to train their models without permission.
Authentic Brands Group, the licensing organization that has ownership of both Presley’s music and likeness, is accusing Anthropic of infringing on the rights of 274 songs by Presley. The lawsuit, first reported by Billboard, was filed on Friday.
While AI firms have already faced copyright infringement claims from the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) and music labels such as Sony, Universal and Warner Records, this case represents one of the first major legal challenges brought directly by an artist’s estate against an AI developer. The result could set a broader precedent for how AI companies are allowed to use existing music catalogues.
“The Elvis plaintiffs bring this action to enforce these exclusive rights against the defendant that has built its entire business model based on copyright infringement at a scale never seen before,” lead attorney Richard Busch wrote in the lawsuit.
The lawsuit claims that “from its inception, Anthropic’s AI model, ‘Claude,’ has created infringing output of copyrighted material of virtually every song from every catalog available on the internet”.
It further accuses Anthropic of utilizing 274 of Presley’s songs to train its AI model. These works include Can’t Help Falling in Love, All Shook Up and A Little Less Conversation. The plaintiffs are seeking $150,000 per infringed track, or about $41m (about £31m).
“Even Anthropic’s institution of guardrails (albeit ineffectively) to purportedly limit outputs which infringe upon music copyrights, after being caught, along with its knowledge that its guardrails were ineffective to stop creating outputs which infringed music copyrights, demonstrates that Anthropic knowingly engaged and continues to willfully engage in copyright infringement of others’ musical works,” the lawsuit states.
AI music platforms work by analyzing large amounts of recorded music in order to learn the sounds, structures and expressions of songs, and then allows users to create their own AI-generated music via text or speech prompts.
Musicians have repeatedly expressed concerns that their music and voices are being used without their permission by AI models, as well as fears that AI-generated “slop” music could replace human-made songs.
Some AI bots have even begun impersonating real living artists on music streaming platforms. Last week, music streaming giant Spotify announced it had removed about 50m songs considered AI slop from its recommendations to users over the past year.

ai-427cb7b893.headline: Is India losing the AI edge? Global Skills Report 2026 ranks nation 40th in workforce readiness
ai-427cb7b893.fulltext:
The global race for artificial intelligence dominance is not just about computing power or capital; it is fundamentally about human capability. According to the newly released Global Skills Report 2026 by Coursera and Udemy, a stark "readiness disconnect" is threatening to derail global AI investments, with the report revealing that 88% of leaders believe their planned AI investments will fail without greater investment in human skills training.
Drawing on data from over 300 million learners across 98 countries, the report introduces the world’s first AI-Human Skills Synergy Index, measuring how effectively nations are building technical AI proficiency alongside the human capabilities—like critical thinking, ethics, and complex problem-solving—required to govern and apply AI safely. 
While Europe leads the global pack, the report serves as a critical wake-up call for India. Ranking 40th out of 98 countries, India finds itself in the "Competitive" tier, trailing significantly behind its Asian peers and highlighting urgent implications for the nation's position in the future global economy.
The Global "Readiness Disconnect
The report paints a picture of a world where AI deployment is vastly outpacing workforce readiness. While nearly three in four organizations have deployed or are piloting AI, only 18% report that most of their workforce participated in AI reskilling last year. 
"AI deployment is outpacing the skills people need to use it effectively," the report notes, highlighting that realizing AI's projected $22.5 trillion economic value by 2031 will require a dual approach. As Andrew Ng, Founder of DeepLearning.AI, states in the report: "Succeeding in these expanded roles will require a combination of AI skills plus broad and deep skills in their specific discipline."
Consequently, learners are urgently pivoting toward human skills that safeguard AI outputs. Global enrollments in **Critical Thinking surged by 107% year-over-year**, while Complex Problem-Solving grew by 126%. 
India’s Ranking: A Wake-Up Call for the IT Giant
In the AI-Human Skills Synergy Index, India secured the 40th position, placing it in the middle-tier "Competitive" rankings (26–50). 
While India avoids the "Lagging" tier (76–98) dominated by parts of Sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America, its 40th-place standing is a sobering metric for a nation that brands itself as the world’s back office and a premier global IT talent hub. 
How India compares to the world?
- The European Juggernaut: Europe dominates the index, with 25 of its 31 countries in the top half. Germany (1st) and France (2nd) lead globally, driven by coordinated EU policies, the AI Act, and massive digital innovation hubs.
- The Asian Peers: India trails significantly behind its regional counterparts and global tech hubs. Japan (3rd), South Korea (4th), the UAE (6th), and Singapore (10th) all rank in the top 10, showcasing strong alignments between national AI infrastructure, policy, and learner skill-building.
- The US Context: The United States (8th) and Canada (11th) also comfortably outpace India, reflecting deeper enterprise integration of AI governance and applied technical skills.
Implications for India: Moving Up the AI Value Chain
India’s 40th-place ranking carries profound economic and strategic implications for the country's massive technology and services sector. 
1. Risk of the "Low-Value AI Trap"
The report cites PwC research indicating that 74% of AI’s economic value is captured by just 20% of organizations. If India’s workforce primarily focuses on foundational AI literacy or routine coding without developing high-level human skills, the country risks being relegated to low-margin, easily automatable tasks in the global AI supply chain (such as basic data labeling or entry-level prompt execution). To capture high-value economic returns, Indian IT firms must transition toward AI product strategy, security, and agentic workflows.
2. The Human Skills Deficit in Entry-Level Roles
A crucial finding in the report is that "leadership skills are expected for AI-exposed entry-level roles." The report notes that in AI-exposed roles, new tasks are 2.5 times more likely to require judgment, empathy, and creativity. For India, which produces millions of entry-level engineering graduates annually, the implication is clear: technical proficiency alone is no longer enough. Indian educational institutions and corporate training programs must urgently integrate critical thinking, ethics, and stakeholder alignment into their core curricula to prevent a massive employability crisis.
3. The Micro-Credential Opportunity
The report highlights that AI micro-credential enrollments grew by 122% globally, with 95% of employers viewing them as key differentiators in hiring. India’s higher education system and corporate sector have a massive opportunity to leverage industry-aligned micro-credentials to signal workforce readiness to global clients, bypassing the slow pace of traditional degree redesigns.
4. Policy and Infrastructure Alignment
The Synergy Index blends learner behavior with national AI readiness. Countries like the UAE and Singapore rank highly because their national strategies pair aggressive infrastructure investment with accessible learning pathways. For India to climb the index, government initiatives must go beyond hardware and broadband; they must heavily subsidize and integrate recognized, applied AI learning pathways that connect directly to sector-specific workforce needs.
The Path Forward for Indian Leaders
The Global Skills Report 2026 offers a clear roadmap for Indian business, education, and government leaders to close the synergy gap:
- For Business Leaders: Move beyond mandatory foundational AI literacy. Build role-specific pathways that combine AI practice with human capabilities like AI security, governance, and complex problem-solving. Treat training as a compliance and risk-mitigation strategy, especially as global clients adopt stringent frameworks like the EU AI Act.
- For Higher Education: Require students to critique AI-supported work, verify evidence, and address ethical consequences. Embed micro-credentials to accelerate curriculum updates and make career-relevant skills visible to global employers.
- For Government: Pair national AI ambitions with accessible skills pathways. Fund workforce development that combines AI proficiency with employability, ensuring that India's demographic dividend is equipped to direct the AI revolution, rather than just participate in its lowest tiers.
As Anthony Salcito, SVP & President of Enterprise at Coursera, concludes in the report's foreword: "AI will continue to change the nature of our work. Our responsibility is to ensure people have the right skills to approach, and direct, that change with confidence." For India, the clock is ticking to ensure its workforce is ready to lead, not just follow, the next era of global technology.

deep-tech-889d13ab65.headline: From 40% to fully Indian: WB Group VP on transfer of technology for Ukraine-Russia tested drones
deep-tech-889d13ab65.fulltext:
Adam Bartosiewicz, Vice-president, WB Group, who was part of a delegation which accompanied Poland Prime Minister Donald Trust during his visit to New Delhi from last week, exclusively spoke to businessline pitching that different classes of Ukraine-Russia battle hardened drones that his company produces could give New Delhi a crucial shortcut to ultimate combat readiness. Edited excerpts of the interview:
You already have a joint venture in India. What exactly are you looking at in India in terms of industrial engagement?
I think our main goal is to somehow establish India as a drone champion, as we are in our part of Europe, based on the extensive experience we have in the application of our products in the Ukraine-Russia conflict and support we provided to the Ukrainian army for fighting since 2014. This means that there is no other company in the world that really gathered that kind of experience over that long period of time. We have kind of stopped counting flight hours of our equipment after one million. Based on this operational experience and lots of feedbacks that we got from the front lines, we have been able to really make war great products. And I think that it would be a very good opportunity for India to jump to that level of combat readiness of the equipment that they intend to also procure in the future.
India is pushing for localising the technology. How much of a percentage of the ToT you are willing to transfer because the cutoff is 60 percent here under Make in India category defence product?
As I said, there is a core technology that has a value in starting the production here. That core technology can be used to build on top of it certain variants of different aspects of a drone. Like, different mission packages for drones and maybe for the use of artificial intelligence. Any other indigenous capabilities that the nation has already demonstrated, we may be a catalyser of internal growth of these technologies. To start with, we may be a good source of knowledge for the Indian Army, based on what we have learned in Ukraine, and also due to the operational experience that Ukrainian army has given us. So we can be sort of a good drone academy for Indian Army.
Can you quantify ToT in terms of a percentage which you are willing to offer?
I think to start with, it will be something like maybe 40 per cent. In a very short time, it may reach 60 per cent. And I would not exclude a scenario where eventually in a matter of years, it can be fully Indian product. As I said, it’s a very big market, and a country with big ambitions and things like our government tries to protect their own companies, like our presence here. We should understand that the same way the government of India will work in the future.
Are you participating in drone acquisition trials?
That particular part we would not like to discuss. However, answering your question, it has been tested at higher altitudes. We have some lessons from the ongoing conflicts and we are sticking to our tactical parameters.
How confident are you, in terms of getting contracts here, to back your investment of $100 million in next 3 years?
As I observed earlier, won’t talk much on this aspect. There’s going to be sort of redefining moment here. What drones are going to be used for? If you observe carefully the changes of situation in the war front in Ukraine, which we follow very closely, the drones of 2022 are no longer useful. And the drones of today operate in completely different ways than before. So the real challenge is not to design drones for today. But to really see what will be the advantage for tomorrow. And we are well prepared for this. Because we have a track record of working with small drones, when nobody in the world was doing that. We have used small drones for coordination of artillery, when nobody in the world was doing that. So, we have seen the future.
You said you want to make India a champion of drones. What is the blue print to bring your niche technology into India?
First of all, India has a huge army with lots of operational needs. And it has already identified drones as a leading technology that is needed to master. So there will be a huge demand for drones in India. That’s one factor. Second factor is that India is a very ambitious country which also has very ambitious people who possess lots of skills in terms of development of technology and capabilities of manufacturing. So you need to take that into account, otherwise, you will not make business here. We think that we will use, first, the existing demand, and existing supply of skilled workforce. That will not only be involved in production but later on in modernisation, and adding certain features from technical standpoint that the Indian Army will be formulating, based on their own experience with absolute good application of the product. So, we see in India a market that is maybe even bigger than the Ukraine or even Europe. In the future, we want to be ready, in order to support this market.
What lessons do you think the Indian forces can imbibe from Russia-Ukraine war, especially in context of use of drone and counter drone systems?
That’s one of our core businesses to link and mix all the different types of technology into one system. So drones in our philosophy just don’t end on drones, on anything that’s flying. It’s simply a combination of many features and many functions that allow armies to win wars. It’s electronic warfare. It’s a combination of the drone application for targeting of different effectors - artillery being on one of them. So this kind of system thinking, I think is a very valuable experience that Indian army can take advantage of.
Your drone was used in Operation Sindoor as well as they continue to be deployed in the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Is there any operational difference between the two war theaters?
Of course, these are two different sets of environment. Ukraine is mostly flat and often demands low altitudes of flights. In case of India, it’s a mixture of different environments, including very high mountains. For that applications, I think we have designed a perfect plane, which is really capable of flying at high altitudes. So there is a sort of reward for us to design perfect planes.
The biggest challenge unmanned systems are facing is operating in contested environment? That challenge is multiplying. How do you address that?
We have encountered these kind of challenges early on, before most of the industry could realise that because we operated in Russia from 2014. So we had no other choice but to factor in these kind of challenges into the design. More than that, based on this operational experience, we have added several other layers of resilience in order to navigate in the GPS denied environment, and also to increase the robustness of the data link, in presence of interferences introduced by the enemy. It’s a very widely circulated opinion that our FlyEye has the best capabilities in terms of avoiding jamming, in terms of communication, and also, it navigates with very decent accuracy.
Are you also facing a situation somewhat like Israel which is shifting some of it’s defense manufacturing to India because whole of the region has come under attack? Similarly, Poland is also facing an attack from Russia.
It’s not the primary, but of course, every factor needs to be taken into account.

Despite US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s optimism that 99 per cent of the deal is complete and an announcement could follow within weeks, the India-US interim trade pact remains stalled over Washington’s insistence on higher import tariffs, with New Delhi unwilling to accept anything more than the additional 10 per cent levy Indian exports currently face, sources said.
Beyond the commercial impasse, India is weighing the domestic political implications of agricultural concessions that the Donald Trump administration hopes to showcase to voters in Republican-leaning states ahead of the US mid-term elections, sources said.
New Delhi believes an agreement is not feasible under the present tariff scenario and the US asks on agriculture, and is inclined to wait until the mid-term elections are over before deciding how to proceed, a source tracking the matter told businessline.
“At this moment, it is not economically feasible for India to accept tariffs greater than the current 10 per cent imposed on its exports under Section 301 (prohibition against forced labour imports). Also, it makes no sense to sign a deal two weeks before the mid-term elections in the US, telling everybody that we are going to sign an agreement fundamentally including products which come from the red states (ones that support US President Donald Trump). This will not fly politically in India,” the source said.
Washington wants to retain the 18 per cent rate envisaged in the February framework, but India sees little reason to accept it when the current additional levy on Indian exporters is 10 per cent, imposed under Section 301 ruling linked to forced labour concern. The tariff situation changed dramatically after the framework was announced on February 7 as the US Supreme Court invalidating reciprocal tariffs imposed by the Trump regime, making the older terms unacceptable.
“Even if the US decides to be flexible and brings down proposed tariffs on India to below 18 per cent, say to 14 per cent or even 12 per cent, there is no way that India could accept it given the fact that the current levels are 10 per cent. And one wouldn’t expect Washington to go below the existing 10 per cent as it would be totally unpopular with certain vote banks,” the source said.
India is also seeking assurances that if additional tariff penalties are imposed on India, for instance under the Russia sanctions legislation or the Section 301 excess-capacity investigation, these would add up to levies lower than those on competing countries, such as Vietnam, Bangladesh and Indonesia, and that no fresh tariffs will follow after the signing. Washington has yet to respond satisfactorily, the source said.
“For New Delhi, accepting agricultural concessions alongside a higher tariff burden could be difficult to defend domestically right now. So, the deal must wait till there is more clarity on the political situation in the US,” the source said.

Large NBFCs and core investment companies (CIC) like Tata Sons and others are required to be registered with the RBI because of the systemic risks, because they sit on top of group companies where they leverage funds and they use the balance sheets of the group companies to return those funds, he said at the NDTV World Summit on Friday. "So, the funds of the public, whether it is through corporate bonds, banks and other means, that is at risk...so, it is for these reasons that these CICs, or NBFCs, are required to be registered," he said. CICs that do not have direct or indirect access to public funds are exempt from the registration requirement, he said. "As long as it is an NBFC within our definition, it is a CIC, it has access to funds, direct or indirect, it's required to be registered, and if it is in the upper layer, then it is required to list," he said. Last month, the RBI rejected Tata Sons' application to surrender its non-banking finance company (NBFC) licence, which will force a public listing of the holding company of the salt-to-software conglomerate Tata Group. This makes a public listing of Tata Sons imminent as it qualifies as an upper layer NBFC, which must mandatorily list on the stock exchanges. Tata Sons was placed in the upper layer in September 2022. It had applied in March 2024 to surrender its registration, and had repaid its debt in an effort to qualify for deregistration. The Tata Sons board has since moved ahead with steps linked to a possible public listing, while saying it will examine other options amid a deepening row within the conglomerate. Malhotra reaffirmed the central bank's primary objective is maintaining price stability with inflation targeting while supporting long-term economic growth. The Tata Sons board has been split over the holding company going public. At a board meeting on September 17, four directors voted in favor of initiating the public listing process, while Noel Tata, the Chairman of Tata Trusts, which holds ~66% of Tata Sons, opposed it.
