india-2bf2eb16d5.fulltext:
Bangladesh per capita GDP forecast to outstrip India’s: What does it mean?
Bangladesh is expected to surpass India’s per capita GDP this year, but the complete economic picture is a mix of success stories and new challenges.
Bangladesh’s per capita gross domestic product (GDP) is projected to be higher than that of Asia’s third largest economy, India, this year, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
GDP is a measure of all goods and services produced within a country during a specific period. India’s GDP is nearly eight times larger than Bangladesh’s. But its neighbour’s per capita GDP, which is GDP divided by the total population, is expected to surpass that of India, the world’s most populous nation.
The projected 2026 per capita GDP of Bangladesh, home to about 175 million people, is $2,886, compared with $2,749 in India as Dhaka emerges as one of South Asia’s notable economic success stories over the past two decades. Bangladesh’s economy is currently larger than that of Pakistan, from which Dhaka seceded in 1971.
Experts link the rise to the country’s $38bn garment industry, remittances and growing participation of women in the workforce.
But high inflation and slowing growth are now putting that progress under pressure. Meanwhile, the Indian economy is expected to grow by 7 percent this year, compared with 3.6 percent in Bangladesh.
So how should one read these numbers, and what do they really mean for millions of people living in these countries?
What’s in the IMF report?
The IMF’s October 2026 World Economic Outlook report underscores differences in how the Indian and Bangladeshi economies are reacting to inflation and the economic pressures caused by two major wars that have jolted energy markets.
Bangladesh is expected to have a GDP of $506.4bn in 2026, compared with India’s $4.15 trillion. But its lead in GDP per capita reverses when adjusted for purchasing power parity (PPP), which accounts for differences in local prices. On this measure, India is projected to have a GDP per capita at $12,998, compared with Bangladesh’s $10,884.
PPP is an economic metric that represents what money can actually buy in different countries after adjusting for the cost of living. The figures mean that Indians have a higher buying capacity than Bangladeshis.
The IMF projected India’s average consumer-price inflation at 5 percent, compared with 8.7 percent in Bangladesh, pointing to greater cost-of-living pressures in Dhaka.
India is relatively wealthier than Bangladesh and is home to a big industrial base, including its significant technology sector.
India’s economy is expected to grow by 7 percent in 2026, nearly twice Bangladesh’s 3.6 percent rate.
For context, the average per capita GDP in developing economies is about $7,746 – and the global average is about $15,889 – against Bangladesh’s $2,886 and India’s $2,749.
Where are India’s and Bangladesh’s economies expected to go?
In the next year, the IMF report projected that Bangladesh’s per capita GDP would reach $3,219, still higher than India’s $3,036 – a difference, according to the estimates, that should continue marginally in 2028.
In 2029, based on current growth forecasts, India’s per capita GDP of $3,661 would top Bangladesh’s $3,334, according to the IMF.
Experts noted that Bangladesh is facing a weaker near-term growth outlook, even as its projected GDP per capita edges above India’s.
But GDP per capita alone does not paint a complete economic picture because it conceals inequalities in income and wealth distribution. The dollar-denominated figure also changes with the exchange rate, which means that a change in a currency’s value can alter the relative numbers without a change in economic output.
In brief, the growth in Bangladesh’s economy in the past two decades has focused on export-oriented manufacturing, particularly its ready-made garment industry, which has been a major source of export earnings and employment, in addition to remittances from Bangladeshis working abroad.
Meanwhile, India has a diversified economy, with services playing a major role alongside manufacturing and agriculture. Its domestic market, technology and business services, industrial base and consumer demand provide multiple sources of economic activity.
In both countries, however, economic growth over the past decade has been unequal with increasing concentration in wealthier households.
Is Bangladesh a South Asian success story?
To some extent, yes, analysts said while expressing caution about unequal growth.
Santosh Mehrotra, an Indian economist, told Al Jazeera that Bangladesh’s economy has shown consistent economic growth of 6 percent per annum alongside a long-term decline in population growth.
The country has also seen its manufacturing contribution to gross value added shoot up from 16.6 percent in 2014 to 22 percent in 2025, Mehrotra said. On the other hand, World Bank data showed India’s manufacturing value added falling from 15.1 percent of GDP in 2014 to 13.5 percent in 2024.
“That’s a positive side of export-oriented manufacturing growth that Bangladesh is getting right,” he said.
However, the global energy shock from the United States-Israel war on Iran, which has disrupted maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, has jolted Bangladesh.
Bangladesh imports 95 percent of its oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), and much of these imports comes from the Middle East.
The ready‑made garment industry, which accounts for more than 80 percent of Bangladesh’s export earnings, has also been hit as its shipment routes via the Red Sea and the Middle East have been disrupted.

world-7a695e6a87.headline: Brazil runoff live updates: ballot count resumes after two-hour voting extension
world-7a695e6a87.fulltext:
Scratch that. Brazilian supreme court justice Cristiano Zanin has just ordered voting in the country’s presidential runoff on Sunday to be extended by two hours, granting a request from Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s campaign.
Polls were initially set to close at 5pm Brasília time. Lula’s campaign alleged that authorities in several cities were restricting voter access to public transportation.
The decision follows allegations of attempted voter suppression in at least 10 states, where public transport appears to have been severely limited in what some suspect was a deliberate ploy to stop Lula voters reaching polling stations.
Earlier, Lula told reporters he had never before complained about elections he had been involved in, irrespective of whether he had won or lost. “But this time something abominable is happening.”
However, some polling stations may have already closed since the decision came so shortly after they were due to close. People should now be able to vote until 7pm.
Lula’s main bet in trying to overturn Bolsonaro’s lead was to increase turnout, after abstention reached a record high in the first round – which, according to many polls, disproportionately affected the leftist’s voters, who generally live farther from polling stations.
The figures are not yet final, but with 24.4% of polling stations counted, they indicated an abstention rate of 19.38%, down from 21.08% in the first round.
Abstention usually rises in Brazilian runoffs – the only exception was in 2022, when the tight contest between Lula and Jair Bolsonaro brought more voters to the polls in the final round.
Meanwhile, hundreds of Lula supporters have camped out on Paulista Avenue to watch the vote count, which started at 7pm local time.
Among them is Camilo Buarque, 35, who came with a bright red banner reading: “Lula: My President”.
“I feel so very happy being here and being here fighting for Lula,” Buarque says, predicting his leader will beat Bolsonaro.
“My confidence comes from the energy and the happiness and the love of these people [around me]. This is democracy,” Buarque says as the first results come in, giving Lula the lead. Fireworks exploded in the air above him as the crowd celebrated the early lead.
João Felipe, a 27-year-old logistics worker, is also there waiting for what he hopes will be a huge Lula party.
“I’ve always been poor and Lula was a very important person when it came to helping people improve their lives,” he says.
“Lula is going to turn this election around. Long live democracy,” Felipe predicts.
“My heart is beating a thousand beats a second but I’m confident,” said his partner, Ester Almeida, 28.
Flávio Bolsonaro is following the count from the mansion of one of his campaign coordinators in a wealthy area of the capital, Brasília. The dozens of journalists present are being kept separate from Bolsonaro and allied politicians, but from time to time they can hear bursts of celebration – like after a goal – whenever the count is updated and Bolsonaro narrows the gap with Lula.
When, with 13.65% of the vote counted, Flávio moved just slightly ahead with 50.01%, an AI-generated funk track began playing loudly and the senator’s guests started chanting a line commonly heard in Brazilian football stadiums: “Go at him, Flávio.”
And just like that, the race is already tightening further. Bolsonaro now has 50.01% of the vote, while Lula has 49.99% of the vote with just over 13.5% of ballots counted.
One of the most popular figures in Flávio Bolsonaro’s party, congressman Nikolas Ferreira, indicated that the far right could use the extension of voting hours as grounds to challenge the election result in the event of a victory by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
Speaking to journalists outside the mansion in Brasília where Bolsonaro was due to follow the count, Ferreira said that “the only person harmed” by the extension was the senator – without, however, mentioning the voters who, as reports throughout the day showed, had been unable to vote because they had no transport.
“The extension only helps whoever is losing,” said the 30-year-old politician who, in the first round, became the most-voted federal congressman in Brazilian history, with 3.1 million votes. He added that justice Cristiano Zanin “wanted to disrupt the election” by issuing the ruling.
Bolsonaro’s campaign chief, senator Rogério Marinho, echoed that line and called the justice’s ruling an “intervention”.
“I sincerely hope common sense prevails and that any judicial coup or administrative manoeuvre does not succeed, for the sake of democracy,” he posted on social media.
Now two hours after the initial extension, polls have officially closed in Brazil (save for another surprise extension). Ballot count has begun.
Although voting time was extended across the country, some polling stations had already closed by the time that decision was announced. As Brazil uses electronic voting machines, once they are closed, they cannot be re-opened.
It’s not clear if certain polling stations had restrictions on if people who arrived after the initial deadline were allowed to vote, as rules usually stipulate that only people in line can still vote after the polls close.
The fact that ballot counting was already underway when the polls were suddenly ordered to remain open has led to some confusion and concerns about the integrity of the election results.
Battle over Meta’s alleged Bolsonaro bias intensified before presidential runoff
Tiago Rogero
Five days after his defeat in the first round of the Brazilian presidential election, leftwing president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva spent almost 24 hours unable to boost his Instagram posts, while his opponent, far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, could.
Lula’s lawyers included the episode in a list of incidents that they submitted to the electoral court and international observers as “evidence” that Meta, Instagram’s owner, was actively trying to interfere in Brazil’s election in Bolsonaro’s favour.
Reports from Lula supporters saying their content had been removed or its reach restricted flooded social media in Brazil, while about a dozen watchdogs and research groups published reports describing what they called “indications” that Meta may have favoured the senator’s campaign.
Meta called Lula’s allegations “false and unfounded”, saying there had been “technical incidents” that affected campaigns from “different parts of the political spectrum”.
The controversy fuelled the electoral battle between Lula and Bolsonaro and gained further traction after the electoral court ordered Meta not to give the candidates “unequal treatment”.
Lula supporters are starting to gather on Paulista Avenue, at the heart of São Paulo, in anticipation of a Lula victory.
The mood is upbeat but tense, amid suspicions that there has been a deliberate pro-Bolsonaro campaign to sabotage public transport systems to stop Lula voters reaching polling stations across the country.
Many people on Paulista Avenue outside the iconic São Paulo Museum of Art suspect foul play from Bolsonaro-supporting politicians and business people.
“I think it’s another coup attempt that the extreme right is trying in Brazil. But we need to really fight so we can win,” said Lucas Lopes, a 32-year-old from São Paulo who works with public relations.
“I’m really worried but I’m optimistic,” Lopes added as dozens of Lula supporters blocked the roads and danced with banners and flags.
“It’s a coup,” agreed Caio Marques, a 40-year-old photographer from Franca, a city in the interior of São Paulo state. “Their arrogance is such that they think they have already won and can do whatever they please and won’t be punished.”
Marques’s partner, Gabriela Leôncio, said: “They are [stopping] public transport in strategic places where Lula has historically had more votes. Where Lula has an advantage, people haven’t managed to get to their polling stations ... They are trying several different types of coup.”
Marques predicted the ploy would fail. “I have faith it won’t [work] because the left is really mobilized,” he said. “I’ll be sincere: in the first round the left failed. But in the second round they woke up ... and there is no coup that will take this away from us.”
Could highly organised pop fans clinch victory for Brazil’s Lula?
Felipe Maia
Earlier this month, Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, led a rally in São Paulo, as he aims to be re-elected to a fourth presidential term, and faces serious opposition from rightwinger Flávio Bolsonaro. Taking the mic before a crowd on Avenida Paulista that organisers put at more than a million, the former union leader began: “I’m not sure whether to open this speech with ‘comrades’ or ‘fandoms from all over Brazil’.” The rally was organised by Lula’s Workers’ party (PT) and a string of other leftwing groups – but the spark came from pop music fandoms.
More than 600 Brazilian fanbase groups for Billie Eilish, Lady Gaga, Katseye, Demi Lovato, Harry Styles, Katy Perry, Selena Gomez, as well as Brazilian stars such as Anitta, Marina Sena and Ludmilla among others, all came together to back Lula, waging an intense online campaign as soon as Lula’s rival, son of imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro, came out on top in the first round on 4 October.
When the first round results came in, “I had this feeling I’d seen it all before with Jair Bolsonaro, and that was really frustrating,” says V, an Eilish fan who helps run Info Billie Brasil, one of the country’s biggest fan communities dedicated to the US singer. “So my first reaction was to use the only communication tool we have and get our community to embrace the cause: Lula’s re-election.”

world-c8d839f31a.headline: Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap?
world-c8d839f31a.fulltext:
Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap?
- Published
Ukraine is in desperate need of a new satellite internet service, but a fast and reliable alternative to Elon Musk's Starlink network simply doesn't exist - yet.
Last week's sudden slowdown of the service in Ukraine, which affected Kyiv's ability to defend itself from Russian attacks, has shown how vulnerable the country can be, and sharply increased Europe's urgency to have its own military-grade satellite network.
That vulnerability was highlighted by Musk himself on Saturday, when he accused Ukraine of violating Starlink's terms of service by using it for "drone strikes to kill people".
Saying that loophole was closed last week, he wrote on X, external: "Violation of those terms will result in end of service."
He added: "Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately".
- How Starlink works on the battlefield 
  - Published15 October
There are a few alternatives, but they are all lagging behind Starlink, which is the world's largest satellite constellation.
France's Eutelsat, with its OneWeb internet service, is the main alternative - but it only has about 600 active satellites, compared with Starlink's 10,000-plus.
The EU is working on a new network to rival Starlink, Iris², however it won't be up and running until 2029.
For Ukraine's troops on the ground, several of whom spoke anonymously to the BBC, reliable connectivity is the difference between life and death.
"God forbid they shut it off completely, it would be an absolute catastrophe," said one. "I don't give a damn how much an alternative costs when our lives are on the line."
For now, Ukraine's best bet is to join Govsatcom, the EU's satellite sharing network - but it cannot be used for military warfare like controlling drones.
Why does Starlink dominate in Ukraine?
Starlink and its military-grade service, Starshield, are both owned by Musk's SpaceX company and have dominated the global satellite market for years.
Ukraine relies on Starlink for communications on the battlefield and Starshield, which is controlled by the US government, for military purposes like drone warfare. The network is able to provide fast, real-time connectivity, which is crucial for defence and intercepting Russian attacks.
"You can't employ drone warfare without this kind of high-speed internet connection," said Vincent Tourret, a researcher at the French Institute of International Relations.
Last week's slowdown, which has only just been restored, highlighted the risks of relying on a US provider at a time when tensions between Kyiv and Washington continue to deteriorate.
"Ukraine's defence cannot depend on Trump's or Musk's whims," French MEP, Christophe Grudler, tweeted.
Who authorised the Starlink restrictions is still not clear, with a confusing blame-game ongoing between the Pentagon, Donald Trump and Musk.
While Starlink has been one of Ukraine's greatest assets in this conflict, the "flipside of that dependence" has been exposed, explained Kari Bingen, director of the Aerospace Security Project at CSIS.
"This is a critical military capability that Ukraine relies on, but doesn't control."
Starlink is not the only satellite network Ukraine can access, so if it goes down there are other options - but experts say they aren't as fast, and troops the BBC spoke to agree.
Starlink "gives us the upper hand when it comes to passing commands - even one or two seconds are critical when we can transfer data and orders faster, and you can really feel that advantage on the battlefield", a soldier said.
The terminals used to connect to the satellites are also an important factor. Starlink's are relatively small and lightweight, so they can be fixed to any kind of vehicle or drone.
Eutelsat's terminals "are slightly larger, so they can be fitted on the roof of a car, or on tanks, but they can't necessarily sit on small drones", said Eva Berneke, former CEO of the French satellite company.
They are also about five times more expensive, she added.
What can the EU offer right now?
Rhetoric from the White House - like Trump's scathing criticism of Nato and his threats against Greenland - have given the EU "some pretty brutal alarm bells", Berneke told the BBC.
She had only been at Eutelsat for a month when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and said she noticed a marked change in urgency from European authorities, as they looked to her company to help plug holes left by Starlink if it could not be relied upon.
Comments from Musk have further heightened the need for an alternative: "Be quiet, small man... there is no substitute for Starlink," he tweeted, external at Poland's foreign minister last year, when the politician said he would "look for other suppliers" if SpaceX was unreliable.
Europe has realised its security depends on space, and it must "strengthen its satellite capacities, urgently", a spokesperson for the European Commission told the BBC.
Right now, it has Govsatcom, a network that was set up in January to share existing satellites between EU member states. Ukraine is not a full-fledged member (although it is trying to become one), but the Commission is in talks with Kyiv to join Govsatcom.
But even if Ukraine could connect tomorrow, the network could not be used for warfare operations like piloting drones, which Starshield is used for.
That could change by the start of next year, however, when the European Commission hopes commercial companies, like Eutelsat's OneWeb, will join the programme. This will give Ukraine some - but not all - of its military network needs.
Eva Berneke told the BBC she is confident the company will be able to "support quite a lot of Ukraine's key military needs". But meeting its communications needs is another thing because, as is the case with most countries, they are varied and massive.
Eutelsat could not comment on Govsatcom, but told the BBC that "as the only European operator of a fully operational [Low Earth Orbit] constellation, we are committed to providing resilient connectivity to the businesses, governments and communities we serve".
No timeline has been given for when Ukraine will be able to join the Govsatcom network. When it does it will likely be as a reliable back-up to Starlink and Starshield.
But that's better than nothing, Vincent Tourret said. "If Starlink is shut down, it's good to have another way to stay connected, but it won't be enough for strikes or interceptions, at this stage."
Iris² - The EU's future network
Govsatcom is seen as a short-term safety net, until the stronger and more secure network, Iris², external is up and running in 2029.
The ambitious project (pronounced Iris squared) is Europe's answer to Starlink and Starshield. It will be a defence-first programme, the European Commission says, with a focus on governments, military and emergency services. Ukraine has been guaranteed access to it from day one.
Part of the EU's space programme, the European satellite companies Eutelsat, SES and Hispasat are leading the project in a consortium called SpaceRISE.
It will still have far fewer satellites than Starlink, with 348 across low and medium earth orbit - but that shouldn't be seen as a negative, said Kari Bingen.
"Think about a flash light beaming down - those satellites will be able to cover a greater amount of the Earth, so you need fewer of them," she explained. "They're all trade offs - I would not take it as a negative, that Iris² is planning for less satellites."
Tourret was more sceptical: "It's no gamechanger and no great saviour, I'm afraid".
A highly produced video on the EU Space Policy's website declares: "With Iris², Europe will no longer depend on others for satellite connectivity."
So does that mean Ukraine could switch off Starlink? No - that wouldn't be a good idea.
"Users need to think about communications resilience," Bingen said. "So if something happens to one system, you have other ways to maintain connectivity."
It's similar to how mobile phones work, explained Eva Berneke: "If you don't have 5G, you go back to 4G. And if you don't have 4G, you might use 3G, so you have multiple networks for resilience. It's the same idea in warfare."
But while a phone might not load pictures as quickly on 3G, for a drone operator, it can be deadly: "That is not a nice situation to have to be in when you're fighting a war."
Iris² is not the only option. This week, Finnish companies Nokia and ICEYE, external announced they would look at developing satellite communications for Ukraine's military defences.
And a joint venture between European satellite makers Airbus, Leonardo and Thales, called Project Bromo, is hoped to be another competitor against SpaceX, but it is still in the very early phases.
Space projects take a long time, Berneke said, and need "a lot of money".
Designing the programme, making the satellites, launching them and then having enough of them in orbit for full coverage takes many years.
"Even if you gave me €8bn right now, I don't think I could have anything up there before 2032-2033," she explained.
Why Space is the new defence frontier
Military work in Space is nothing new, and has been happening since the dawn of the space age in the 1950s. But the conflict in Ukraine has shown how integral it is to modern warfare.
"Communication is so important, and terrestrial communication platforms, whether it's 5G or fibre, can be attacked on the ground," Berneke said. "It is a lot harder to shoot down an entire satellite network. That's not something any military can do right now."
While we look to the skies, however, most of the world's communications are travelling via undersea cables - about 99% in fact. But these are vulnerable to attack - this week the UK government outlined new measures to protect its cables, after an increase in suspicious activity by Russian vessels.
"In a crisis or conflict, there are serious concerns that undersea cables will be cut... so if that happens it's good to have satellite communication as a backup," Kari Bingen said.

health-tech-db8b4a5a7f.fulltext:
The shift comes as Indian research into lower-dose regimens offers another potential route to reducing treatment costs. Together, cheaper drug alternatives and evidence-based dosing strategies could widen access to advanced cancer treatment, although affordability at the manufacturer's end does not guarantee that patients will benefit at the hospital counter.
Dr Imran Shaikh of Kokilaben Dhirubhai Ambani Hospital in Mumbai told TOI that his nivolumab prescriptions had risen by more than 50% over the past six months.
“My patients are responding well to the drug. People who were earlier unsure whether they could afford a cycle costing over a lakh of rupees are comfortable with the new price tag of Rs 30,000,” he said.
From a costly option to a broader treatment window
The change matters in a country where access to immunotherapy has historically been limited by price. A Tata Memorial Centre (TMC) study found that only 2.8% of patients eligible for immunotherapy were receiving it in 2022. Dr Jyoti Bajpai, director of precision oncology at Apollo Hospitals in Navi Mumbai and a co-author of the study, said prescriptions have since risen substantially, though the overall increase is yet to be quantified.
Nivolumab belongs to a class of drugs called immune checkpoint inhibitors, which help the body's immune system recognise and attack cancer cells. Its use across multiple tumour types makes the availability of a less expensive version particularly significant. TMC doctors say the drug is effective across 25 tumour types and has about 100 indications.
The benefits can be substantial for eligible patients. Dr Kumar Prabhash, head of medical oncology at Tata Memorial Hospital in Mumbai's Parel, cited melanoma, or skin cancer, as an example of the difference immunotherapy has made.
“Earlier barely five out of 100 patients had long-term survival, but survival has now increased to 50% with immunotherapy,” he said, adding that some patients with advanced lung cancer are surviving for five years or longer.
In certain cases, the treatment may also spare patients more invasive interventions. Patients with early-stage colorectal cancer carrying high microsatellite instability (MSI-high), a biomarker that can help predict response to immunotherapy, may be able to avoid the conventional combination of chemotherapy, radiotherapy and surgery.
“A patient of MSI-high type of colon cancer would earlier need chemotherapy, radiotherapy and surgery. But if he comes in early stages, then only immunotherapy works. The patient will have his native organ intact,” Prabhash said.
Cheaper at the factory, but will patients pay less?
The price of nivolumab could fall further, with four additional versions expected to enter the market. Yet competition alone may not be enough to ensure that patients receive the least expensive option.
Shaikh said India has only seven checkpoint inhibitor drugs available, compared with 35 in China. The other six available in India, apart from nivolumab, are imported and can cost lakhs of rupees over a course of treatment.
A separate policy intervention could help ease the wider cost burden. The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority's decision to cap trade margins on 137 anti-cancer medicines, effective November 8, is projected to generate annual savings of Rs 2,500 crore. The measure could reduce costs across several cancer treatments, though the actual savings for patients will depend on how the price controls translate into retail prices and hospital purchasing practices.
K M Gopakumar of Third World Network warned that hospitals requiring patients to buy medicines from their in-house pharmacies could have little incentive to stock lower-priced alternatives if the margins are less attractive.
“Hospitals may favour more expensive original medicines because of higher margins. The cheaper versions may thus not be available to the patients as a result,” he said.
The same concern applies to nivolumab as more biosimilars enter the market. Gopakumar said the price could drop from Rs 30,000 to Rs 10,000, but questioned whether hospitals would stock products that offer them lower margins.
Prabhash said TMC tries to keep medicine costs as low as possible for patients. Whether similar savings reach patients across the healthcare system remains an open question.
For Bajpai, the larger opportunity lies in combining affordable biosimilars with treatment strategies backed by clinical evidence. Research into shorter courses and lower doses has explored ways to reduce expenses for patients who might otherwise struggle to complete treatment. More affordable alternatives could make it possible for a greater number of eligible patients to receive full-dose, full-course treatment where clinically appropriate.
“The real success of innovation is not just how long patients live, but how many patients can access the treatment they need — without financial hardship,” she said.

work-careers-38b6f786f5.headline: U.S. immigration restrictions may outlast Trump
work-careers-38b6f786f5.fulltext:
In its second term, the Donald Trump administration has been active in restricting legal immigration to the United States. The administration’s attempt to impose a $100,000 payment requirement on certain new H-1B petitions, changes to visa renewal procedures, the introduction of a wage-weighted selection system, and the latest suspensions of the Program Electronic Review Management (PERM) process are cases in point, disproportionately impacting Indian immigrants and firms.
It is tempting to read these developments as a product of the Trump administration alone, but they reflect deeper political interests that are likely to survive post-Trump. Indian nationals account for 70% of H-1B visa approvals, with one-fifth of the visas going to employees of Indian-origin companies. This means that, as the bipartisan focus on immigration reform continues, the issue is likely to sustain as a friction point in India-U.S. relations.
The views of the Democrats and Republicans
Democrats are expected to dominate the upcoming midterm elections in November. They view immigration through a rights-based lens, and their voters remain supportive of both legal immigration and increased legalisation of undocumented immigrants. Some 75% of Democrats see skilled immigration as good for the U.S., compared with 54% of Republicans. Even under the current administration, Democrats have pushed for easing F-1 student visa requirements and have traditionally enjoyed the support of diaspora communities in the U.S., including the Indian diaspora.
However, prominent Democratic Senators such as Dick Durbin and Richard Blumenthal, as well as progressive Independents such as Bernie Sanders, have also pushed for bills seeking H-1B reforms. Democrats view alleged fraud in the H-1B visa system as a serious challenge that needs to be addressed. Similarly, the labour wing of the Democratic Party views the H-1B visa programme as a potential threat to domestic labour protections and workers’ rights. The Democrats’ immigrant voter base, their open opposition to the H-1B visa fee hikes, and resistance to these restrictions from businesses and unions suggest that a Democratic-controlled Congress may soften the harshest executive measures and tone down the rhetoric. However, concerns about visa fraud and worker protections mean that Democrats are likely to keep up the pressure on the outsourcing model and continue pushing for H-1B reforms.
While a plurality of Republicans support restrictions on legal immigration, this number has declined considerably since 2025. Among the Republican leadership, there is a visible split between anti-immigration nationalists and pro-immigration business interests. The Trump administration’s hikes in the H-1B visa fee is an example of this conflict. While the administration was openly critical of the programme and aggressively pushed for the fee increase, it subsequently diluted the measure by including exemptions for graduates of U.S. universities and existing visa holders, following pressure from businesses and universities.
The business divide
The debate over wage-weighted entries versus the lottery system for H-1B visas has dominated discussions on immigration within the U.S. business community. There are three broad categories in this debate. The first is the random lottery system that was in place until 2026, which benefited outsourcing firms and start-ups. The second is the wage-weighted lottery system (February 2026), which infers wage levels based on experience, job role and location, dividing visa quotas into four categories. On the surface, this system might benefit big-tech firms, but it could also benefit outsourcing firms that hire highly experienced workers for lower wages. The third is the actual wage weighted lottery model, which is supported by U.S.-based industries. This approach could dilute the advantages enjoyed by outsourcing firms while benefiting American hires and also F1 student hires.
For the artificial intelligence (AI) and big-tech business community, this reform could be beneficial in two ways. First, AI graduate programmes and advanced research roles in the U.S. rely heavily on international talent, with demand for AI skills growing faster than the supply of domestic graduates. The reform could therefore help AI firms secure top international talent for higher wages.
Second, the AI sector is expanding into market segments traditionally occupied by start-ups and outsourcing companies, which often perform low technology maintenance and communication roles. The AI sector could therefore benefit if these start-ups and outsourcing firms were compelled to hire fewer workers. With the AI sector playing a prominent role in campaign contributions for the 2026 midterm elections, these policies to counter outsourcing firms are likely to continue. With over 54% of India’s software services exports going to the U.S., which remains the top market for Indian information technology (IT) outsourcing, this represents a major challenge for India. However, these developments could also be viewed as positive news for Indian students at U.S. universities.
Looking ahead
The U.S. Department of Labor’s suspension of eight firms, including not only Indian outsourcing companies such as Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services and Wipro but also major technology firms such as Microsoft and Adobe, from green card sponsorship reinforces this trend. It raises the cost of hiring foreign workers for businesses as a whole, creating pressure that remains largely beyond partisan control.
With Mr. Trump’s political power potentially diminished after November, anti-immigration rhetoric could decline. However, with both parties committed to immigration reform, India should continue to expect an unfavourable and unpredictable immigration landscape.

global-economics-c20facd61e.headline: From 40% to fully Indian: WB Group VP on transfer of technology for Ukraine-Russia tested drones
global-economics-c20facd61e.source: Business News Today: Latest Business News, Finance News
global-economics-c20facd61e.fulltext:
Adam Bartosiewicz, Vice-president, WB Group, who was part of a delegation which accompanied Poland Prime Minister Donald Trust during his visit to New Delhi from last week, exclusively spoke to businessline pitching that different classes of Ukraine-Russia battle hardened drones that his company produces could give New Delhi a crucial shortcut to ultimate combat readiness. Edited excerpts of the interview:
You already have a joint venture in India. What exactly are you looking at in India in terms of industrial engagement?
I think our main goal is to somehow establish India as a drone champion, as we are in our part of Europe, based on the extensive experience we have in the application of our products in the Ukraine-Russia conflict and support we provided to the Ukrainian army for fighting since 2014. This means that there is no other company in the world that really gathered that kind of experience over that long period of time. We have kind of stopped counting flight hours of our equipment after one million. Based on this operational experience and lots of feedbacks that we got from the front lines, we have been able to really make war great products. And I think that it would be a very good opportunity for India to jump to that level of combat readiness of the equipment that they intend to also procure in the future.
India is pushing for localising the technology. How much of a percentage of the ToT you are willing to transfer because the cutoff is 60 percent here under Make in India category defence product?
As I said, there is a core technology that has a value in starting the production here. That core technology can be used to build on top of it certain variants of different aspects of a drone. Like, different mission packages for drones and maybe for the use of artificial intelligence. Any other indigenous capabilities that the nation has already demonstrated, we may be a catalyser of internal growth of these technologies. To start with, we may be a good source of knowledge for the Indian Army, based on what we have learned in Ukraine, and also due to the operational experience that Ukrainian army has given us. So we can be sort of a good drone academy for Indian Army.
Can you quantify ToT in terms of a percentage which you are willing to offer?
I think to start with, it will be something like maybe 40 per cent. In a very short time, it may reach 60 per cent. And I would not exclude a scenario where eventually in a matter of years, it can be fully Indian product. As I said, it’s a very big market, and a country with big ambitions and things like our government tries to protect their own companies, like our presence here. We should understand that the same way the government of India will work in the future.
Are you participating in drone acquisition trials?
That particular part we would not like to discuss. However, answering your question, it has been tested at higher altitudes. We have some lessons from the ongoing conflicts and we are sticking to our tactical parameters.
How confident are you, in terms of getting contracts here, to back your investment of $100 million in next 3 years?
As I observed earlier, won’t talk much on this aspect. There’s going to be sort of redefining moment here. What drones are going to be used for? If you observe carefully the changes of situation in the war front in Ukraine, which we follow very closely, the drones of 2022 are no longer useful. And the drones of today operate in completely different ways than before. So the real challenge is not to design drones for today. But to really see what will be the advantage for tomorrow. And we are well prepared for this. Because we have a track record of working with small drones, when nobody in the world was doing that. We have used small drones for coordination of artillery, when nobody in the world was doing that. So, we have seen the future.
You said you want to make India a champion of drones. What is the blue print to bring your niche technology into India?
First of all, India has a huge army with lots of operational needs. And it has already identified drones as a leading technology that is needed to master. So there will be a huge demand for drones in India. That’s one factor. Second factor is that India is a very ambitious country which also has very ambitious people who possess lots of skills in terms of development of technology and capabilities of manufacturing. So you need to take that into account, otherwise, you will not make business here. We think that we will use, first, the existing demand, and existing supply of skilled workforce. That will not only be involved in production but later on in modernisation, and adding certain features from technical standpoint that the Indian Army will be formulating, based on their own experience with absolute good application of the product. So, we see in India a market that is maybe even bigger than the Ukraine or even Europe. In the future, we want to be ready, in order to support this market.
What lessons do you think the Indian forces can imbibe from Russia-Ukraine war, especially in context of use of drone and counter drone systems?
That’s one of our core businesses to link and mix all the different types of technology into one system. So drones in our philosophy just don’t end on drones, on anything that’s flying. It’s simply a combination of many features and many functions that allow armies to win wars. It’s electronic warfare. It’s a combination of the drone application for targeting of different effectors - artillery being on one of them. So this kind of system thinking, I think is a very valuable experience that Indian army can take advantage of.
Your drone was used in Operation Sindoor as well as they continue to be deployed in the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Is there any operational difference between the two war theaters?
Of course, these are two different sets of environment. Ukraine is mostly flat and often demands low altitudes of flights. In case of India, it’s a mixture of different environments, including very high mountains. For that applications, I think we have designed a perfect plane, which is really capable of flying at high altitudes. So there is a sort of reward for us to design perfect planes.
The biggest challenge unmanned systems are facing is operating in contested environment? That challenge is multiplying. How do you address that?
We have encountered these kind of challenges early on, before most of the industry could realise that because we operated in Russia from 2014. So we had no other choice but to factor in these kind of challenges into the design. More than that, based on this operational experience, we have added several other layers of resilience in order to navigate in the GPS denied environment, and also to increase the robustness of the data link, in presence of interferences introduced by the enemy. It’s a very widely circulated opinion that our FlyEye has the best capabilities in terms of avoiding jamming, in terms of communication, and also, it navigates with very decent accuracy.
Are you also facing a situation somewhat like Israel which is shifting some of it’s defense manufacturing to India because whole of the region has come under attack? Similarly, Poland is also facing an attack from Russia.
It’s not the primary, but of course, every factor needs to be taken into account.

india-1da7929470.headline: India-US interim trade deal remains stuck over tariffs, political concerns, sources
india-1da7929470.fulltext:
Despite US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s optimism that 99 per cent of the deal is complete and an announcement could follow within weeks, the India-US interim trade pact remains stalled over Washington’s insistence on higher import tariffs, with New Delhi unwilling to accept anything more than the additional 10 per cent levy Indian exports currently face, sources said.
Beyond the commercial impasse, India is weighing the domestic political implications of agricultural concessions that the Donald Trump administration hopes to showcase to voters in Republican-leaning states ahead of the US mid-term elections, sources said.
New Delhi believes an agreement is not feasible under the present tariff scenario and the US asks on agriculture, and is inclined to wait until the mid-term elections are over before deciding how to proceed, a source tracking the matter told businessline.
“At this moment, it is not economically feasible for India to accept tariffs greater than the current 10 per cent imposed on its exports under Section 301 (prohibition against forced labour imports). Also, it makes no sense to sign a deal two weeks before the mid-term elections in the US, telling everybody that we are going to sign an agreement fundamentally including products which come from the red states (ones that support US President Donald Trump). This will not fly politically in India,” the source said.
Washington wants to retain the 18 per cent rate envisaged in the February framework, but India sees little reason to accept it when the current additional levy on Indian exporters is 10 per cent, imposed under Section 301 ruling linked to forced labour concern. The tariff situation changed dramatically after the framework was announced on February 7 as the US Supreme Court invalidating reciprocal tariffs imposed by the Trump regime, making the older terms unacceptable.
“Even if the US decides to be flexible and brings down proposed tariffs on India to below 18 per cent, say to 14 per cent or even 12 per cent, there is no way that India could accept it given the fact that the current levels are 10 per cent. And one wouldn’t expect Washington to go below the existing 10 per cent as it would be totally unpopular with certain vote banks,” the source said.
India is also seeking assurances that if additional tariff penalties are imposed on India, for instance under the Russia sanctions legislation or the Section 301 excess-capacity investigation, these would add up to levies lower than those on competing countries, such as Vietnam, Bangladesh and Indonesia, and that no fresh tariffs will follow after the signing. Washington has yet to respond satisfactorily, the source said.
“For New Delhi, accepting agricultural concessions alongside a higher tariff burden could be difficult to defend domestically right now. So, the deal must wait till there is more clarity on the political situation in the US,” the source said.

world-a4dafb4ffd.headline: Volkswagen to build $4bn Audi SUV factory in US despite job cuts at home
world-a4dafb4ffd.fulltext:
Audi has said it will spend $4bn (£3bn) to build its first factory in the US, as its parent company, Volkswagen, struggles with the impact of steep tariffs imposed by Donald Trump.
The German brand’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a campaign rally on Saturday night to announce the factory in Macon, Georgia, in an unusual move by a big European brand just days before the US midterm elections.
The Republican party under Trump is trying to retain control of both houses of Congress, but it is polling poorly as it struggles with higher fuel prices caused by Trump’s war on Iran, as well as his trade war against some of the US’s biggest trading partners.
Trump has long tried to convince voters that his tariffs are helping to increase the number of manufacturing jobs in the US, and has seized on any new factory investments. However, US vehicle and parts employment has fallen since Trump took office last year.
Audi, Volkswagen’s most important premium brand, has suffered from Trump’s 15% tariffs on imports from the EU as well as the president’s efforts to cut sales of battery electric vehicles in favour of petrol cars.
It said it aims to build 200,000 SUVs at the new US factory, creating 4,500 jobs. The factory will build the Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, shifting some production from Bratislava in Slovakia.
Volkswagen has said Trump’s tariffs cost it up to €5bn(£4.2bn)a year, before the impact of lower sales. The German manufacturer this month said it was still struggling with “continued high pressure from import tariffs”. The carmaker was also forced to shift some production of its cheapest cars, such as the Jetta saloon and Taos SUV, from Mexico to the US.
The new factory may add to tensions in Germany, where Volkswagen has started to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories. It has blamed the job losses on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as the tariffs and a need to invest heavily in the shift to EVs for markets other than the US.
Döllner said he accepted the invitation to speak at Trump’s rally out of respect for the US.
“We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” he said at the event. “This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market.”
Volkswagen’s chief executive, Oliver Blume, told investors in July that “US tariffs create a significant burden and restrict international trade”.
However, the group has said there is still demand in the US for Audi’s large petrol SUVs, and it is planning its largest-ever SUV, the Q9, with the American market in mind. Large petrol-powered SUVs have played a big role in global carbon emissions.

other-interests-e8b987c95a.headline: Brazil presidential election dogged by alleged bias by Meta AI tools
other-interests-e8b987c95a.fulltext:
A deluge of AI-generated content and unfair treatment by social media platforms could prove pivotal in Brazil’s presidential election, according to supporters of the left-wing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
Lula will face off against right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro on 25 October in the second round of the contest. Lula’s campaign has formally accused Meta – which owns WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook – of favouring Bolsonaro by suspending Lula’s campaign advertising account, suppressing posts and blocking AI-generated content.
Brazil’s electoral prosecutors have said Meta failed to fully comply with court orders to ensure equal treatment of both candidates, while United Nations human rights experts have said they are concerned by possible unequal treatment of the two campaigns.
Advertisement
Images have widely circulated showing Meta AI, a chatbot integrated into WhatsApp, refusing to generate campaign posters for Lula, while instantly producing an image for “Flávio”.
In a statement, Meta said “claims that we are favoring or interfering on behalf of any candidate or political group are false and unfounded”. It said Lula’s account was suspended for 1 hour by mistake and that its systems blocked prompts referring to the names “Lula” and “Bolsonaro”, but not the common first names Luiz or Flávio.
Lula’s campaign remains unconvinced. It submitted screenshots to the electoral court showing Meta AI repeatedly assigning Bolsonaro’s electoral number, 22, to generic, fictional politicians and allegedly translating “Flávio futuro presidiário” (“Flávio future prisoner”) as “Flávio future president”.
Determining whether the discrepancies are deliberate is impossible because Meta’s systems are opaque, says David Nemer at the University of Virginia. “But when a technical glitch tends to repeat its outcome, it’s very hard to accept that this is just a technical failure.”
Lula finished behind Bolsonaro in the first round of voting, but polls show the gap is narrowing. The comeback has been partly credited to Lula’s Army, an intensive online campaign in which 8 million WhatsApp channel subscribers receive daily tasks, such as posting photographs on Instagram posing with their fingers forming an L.
This year’s general election is Brazil’s first since large language models (LLMs) became widely popular, and it is awash with AI-generated content. Experts say Latin America’s largest democracy offers a glimpse of what is to come for AI in politics.
Fact-checking organisation Lupa identified 920 pieces of AI-generated or manipulated election content ahead of the first round, primarily on Facebook and Instagram, 60 per cent of it unlabelled. Another investigation found that 26 Meta advertising accounts appeared to sidestep restrictions on foreign-funded political advertising by posting AI-generated videos, including one depicting Bolsonaro and Argentina’s president Javier Milei freeing Brazil from communists.
Meta’s independent oversight board says the company’s election safeguards have failed.
“It’s very worrying,” says Nemer. “So much of our political campaign dynamics have been transferred to privatised companies that we have no idea how they operate.”
Regulating AI in political campaigns won’t be as simple as it seems, says Heloísa Massaro at InternetLab, a Brazilian digital rights non-profit that studied how eight major AI chatbots respond to questions about Brazil’s election.
Its report found that chatbots sometimes refused genuine questions about candidates, referring users to official electoral websites, but would agree to draft misleading claims questioning the integrity of elections for use in campaigning.
Massaro says clearer safeguards for LLMs are needed, but first their objectives must be defined.
“Are the safeguards working? That’s one question. But working for what, because it depends on what your goals are,” she says. “Is the solution to send people away without providing any kind of information? Is this what we want?”

world-e189f9f1ed.headline: Brazil election 2026: Live second round results
world-e189f9f1ed.fulltext:
Polls were originally due to close at 17.00BRT, 20.00GMT, but voting was extended for two hours; the full count is now under way. Full coverage here
How the election works
Brazil’s president is elected purely by the popular vote. A winning candidate needs one more vote than 50% of votes cast; there is no role for the parliament and no electoral college.
Because no candidate achieved 50% in the first round on 4 October, the two leading candidates go into a runoff. One of them is Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the incumbent leftwing president, commonly known as Lula. The other, and the leading candidate in the first round, is Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro.
Bolsonaro senior is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a failed coup attempt after he lost to Lula in the 2022 election, but has endorsed his son and hopes to be released if he wins. Bolsonaro junior is a lawyer and former senator from Rio.
In 2022, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro in the second round, with an electoral base concentrated in the north-east of the country, while Bolsonaro led in the south. But on that occasion Lula entered the second round as the leading candidate from the first round, and won the bellwether state of Minas Gerais, north of Rio de Janeiro. In the first round of the 2026 election, Bolsonaro beat Lula in Minas Gerais by 48.43% to 43.33%.
Never, since the return of democracy to Brazil in 1985, has the first round runner-up managed to turn the game around and win the second vote. But Lula’s campaign has been buoyed by massive, student-led anti-Bolsonaro protests after the first round and hopes to stage a historic fightback on Sunday.
Lula is already the longest-serving president in Brazil’s modern history, serving two terms from 2003 to 2010, before returning to office in 2023. He will turn 81 on Tuesday. Bolsonaro is 45.

world-41297b247f.headline: Venezuela’s opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returns from exile
world-41297b247f.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
world-41297b247f.fulltext:
Venezuela’s opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returns from exile
The Nobel laureate’s homecoming follows national protests demanding free elections.
Venezuela’s opposition leader Maria Corina Machado has successfully returned to the country after more than 10 months in exile.
Machado announced her arrival on social media on Sunday, writing, “I am here. With you.”
The current opposition leader, Edmundo Gonzalez, confirmed the news, writing on X that “our leader, my dear Maria Corina, is on Venezuelan soil”.
The Comando Con Venezuela political organisation shared footage of Machado arriving at a church in Lara, where she was greeted by supporters.
Machado first disappeared from public life after being briefly arrested in January 2025. She re-emerged last December in Norway, where she won the Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to challenge Venezuela President Nicolas Maduro. Maduro was abducted from Caracas by the United States military in January 2026.
Venezuela’s Vice President Delcy Rodriguez has stood in as acting president since then, with the endorsement of US President Donald Trump, and has cooperated with his administration regarding reforms in the country, as well as a deal to grant the US control of over 65 billion barrels’ worth of Venezuela’s oil reserves.
Calls for elections to be held
Rodriguez’s presidency has extended far beyond the 90-day period she was authorised to serve following Maduro’s removal. But she has yet to call an election despite public demand and despite her promise to do so at the United Nations General Assembly in September. The US maintains that the country is not ready yet.
Earlier this week, thousands of Venezuelans took to the streets to call for elections in the first nationwide opposition protest in nearly two years.
Although the opposition is widely believed to have won Venezuela’s disputed 2024 elections, Trump has cast doubt on Machado’s abilities to lead, claiming in January that she “doesn’t have the support within or the respect within the country”.
Machado presented Trump with her Nobel medal when visiting him in the White House weeks later, in what she said was “a recognition for his unique commitment with our freedom”. The US leader has repeatedly voiced his desire to be awarded the Nobel Peace Prize himself.
Machado has made previous unsuccessful attempts to enter Venezuela. In September, her team said she had made seven attempts in the space of a few weeks.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced on X that “the conditions allowing for the safe return of Ms. Machado to Venezuela is the direct result of the U.S. supported reconciliation talks which has already seen hundreds of political prisoners freed and hundreds of political opposition figures return from exile.”
Asked to comment about Machado’s return, Trump told reporters on Sunday, “I don’t know anything about it, but I think she’s a very nice woman.”
“She gave me her Nobel Prize, so how can I say anything else? And I hope she’s safe.”

Venezuelan opposition leader María Machado returns after months in exile
Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado has returned home to a fraught political landscape after more than 10 months in exile.
"I am here. With you," Machado wrote on X on Sunday. Her return comes after repeated prior efforts to re-enter the country came to no avail.
In January, a month after Machado left Venezuela on a speedboat under cover of darkness to accept the Nobel Peace Prize in Norway, the US seized her opponent, President Nicolás Maduro.
The Trump administration then backed his deputy, Delcy Rodríguez, as leader and she was sworn in as interim president, later signing an oil deal which granted very favourable terms to the US.
Machado was photographed on Sunday attending Mass at a church in the Venezuelan state of Lara, surrounded by supporters hugging her and clasping her hands.
Her ally, former presidential candidate Edmundo González, confirmed her arrival, writing in a statement: "I am thrilled to announce to you that our leader, my dear María Corina, is on Venezuelan soil."
"Today is a very important day for Venezuelans. Our sovereign voice returns with her to lead and guide this process!" González said.
He added that he will soon join Machado in Venezuela to advance the country "toward freedom".
An advisor to Machado said in September that over the previous few weeks Machado had attempted seven times to return to Venezuela, but was denied each time. There have been reports that the US was involved in delaying her return, which it has denied.
It's unclear what Machado plans to do next now that she's back, but she has previously said she would run for president again if an election were held. Her ability to return to her country was always contingent on approval from the Trump administration, which it appears has now been granted.
A staunch supporter of democracy, Machado won an independent presidential primary election - held outside the Maduro government's official election authority - in 2023, earning more than 90% of the vote.
Despite winning the primary, Maduro's government barred Machado from running for office, accusing her of fraud and tax violations. Machado denied the allegations, calling them politically motivated. She spent her final days in the country hiding in safehouses before her fleeing to Norway to accept the Nobel Prize.
In the 2024 election, Machado's ally González ran in her place against Maduro.
The electoral authority, which is closely aligned with the government, declared Maduro the winner without making detailed voting tallies public.
The opposition argued that González won the election, not Maduro, uploading copies of the voting tallies as evidence.
Maduro was removed from the country by US forces in January, and is currently jailed in New York where he faces drugs, weapons and torture charges. He has pleaded not guilty.
A spokesman for Machado called her return "a major step toward a democratic transition and free, fair, and verifiable presidential elections in the near future".
"We thank President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the US Government, Congress, and allied governments for their continued leadership and support," her spokesperson, David Smolansky, added.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump said, "I don't know anything about" her return, and added that he hoped she was "safe".
"I think she's a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel Prize, so how can I say anything else? And I hope she's safe," he said.
In January, Machado visited the White House and gifted her Nobel prize award to Trump. The committee that issues the prize had said "it cannot be revoked, shared, or transferred to others".
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio praised his country's role in securing her return through political reconciliation talks.
"The conditions allowing for the safe return of Ms Machado to Venezuela is the direct result of the US supported reconciliation talks which has already seen hundreds of political prisoners freed and hundreds of political opposition figures return from exile," he posted on X.
He added: "We expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in thirty years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election but an enduring democracy."

Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returned home on Sunday after nearly a year away, and after several failed attempts to return that strained her ties with US President Donald Trump’s administration.
“I’m here. With you all,” the Nobel Peace Prize-winner wrote on social media.
She appeared at a church in western Lara state, according to images shared by her press team, and was greeted by bystanders who sang the national anthem and shouted “liberty!” as she left in an ‌SUV, a Reuters witness said. She will travel to Caracas by road, her team said.
Her efforts to return have tested her relationship with the Trump administration, which she has sought to cultivate as an ally since before it removed president Nicolas Maduro from power in January.
US officials have asked her at least once to delay her return, Reuters reported in June, and she has made several failed attempts to enter the country. Her team did not disclose details how she returned.
Trump has repeatedly expressed support for interim President Delcy Rodriguez, former deputy to ousted president Nicolas Maduro, and hailed deals on oil production and other business ventures by US companies in the South American country. Trump said in ⁠September it was too soon to consider democratic elections in Venezuela.
At the White House on Sunday, Trump said he did not know anything about Machado’s return and suggested the US ‌would continue to back Rodriguez.
“She’s a very nice woman,” he said, referring to Machado. “But we’re doing really well in Venezuela.”
Machado took a private plane from Panama to Colombia and then crossed overland to Venezuela, two people with knowledge of the matter said.
“The conditions allowing for the safe return ‌of Ms Machado to Venezuela are the direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks which have already seen hundreds of political prisoners freed and hundreds of political ⁠opposition figures return from exile,” US Secretary of ⁠State Marco Rubio said in a statement.
“We expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in 30 years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election but an enduring democracy.”
A ‌faction of the opposition and the interim government held their latest session of talks this month, with the aim of remaking the top court and electoral council, among other goals, ahead of eventual elections. They do not include Machado’s political movement.
The ‌Venezuelan communications ‌ministry, which handles all press queries for the government, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Machado’s return.
“Maria Corina Machado will achieve liberty and democracy in Venezuela,” ‌said Hernan Adames, 69, as he celebrated with other supporters in Barquisimeto.
Machado plans to meet with victims of the deadly earthquakes that struck Venezuela in June, as well as the families ⁠of political prisoners, the international community and various leaders from the democratic movement in Venezuela, David Smolansky, her top foreign affairs adviser, told Reuters.
“She will work proactively for a date for free ⁠and fair elections,” he added.
International energy firms committed last month to expanding projects in the country in a signing ceremony overseen by Rodriguez and US Energy Secretary Chris Wright.
Machado has said that only a “serious, democratic government” can provide the stability needed by investors.
She had been barred by Maduro’s government from exiting Venezuela but she secretly left ‌in late 2025 to receive the Nobel Peace ‌Prize, after spending more than a year living mostly in hiding.
Machado’s Vente Venezuela movement debuted an app on Saturday to collect voter registration information from Venezuelans abroad. The group hopes eventually to share data from the app, which was built by 15 staff over the last 18 months, with a reformed electoral council so users can be officially added to voter rolls.
Edmundo Gonzalez, a former presidential candidate for Machado’s movement who has been living in Spain, said on social media he would soon join her in Venezuela.
